It's easy to see why. A

looks like an array: you index it, slice it and loop over it, and an array converts to one implicitly. Benchmarks show span-based code beating array-and-string code, and indexing a span compiles to code almost identical to indexing an array. Since C# 13, spans are even allowed inside async methods, which looks like the old rules are gone.
But the speed doesn't come from being a better array. It comes from not being an array at all.
A span is a view, not storage
holds two things: a reference to the first element and a length. It owns nothing. The reference can point into a managed array, into a string (for
), into memory allocated on the stack with
, or into native memory. Slicing creates a new reference and length over the same memory, without copying, which is why
allocates a new string. Writes through a span change the memory behind it.
Why it has to stay on the stack
That reference is what makes the rules necessary. If the span points at
memory, that memory disappears when the method returns, so the span can't outlive the method. If it points into the middle of an array, it's an

, which is relatively expensive for the garbage collector to track, so the runtime only allows them on the stack. And a span is two fields, larger than a machine word: on the heap, one thread could read the new reference with the old, longer length, and read past the end of the memory. So
, and the compiler enforces where it may live: not as a field of a class or a normal struct, not as an array element, not boxed, and not captured by a lambda.
